messages.body_plain:
Jasmine,

The Kappa statistic, both univariate and multivariate, have long been misinterpreted. Under Brownian motion, the expected value of K and Kmult is 1.0.  Values larger than this mean there is greater phylogenetic signal than what one might expect under BM, and less than 1.0 there is less phylogenetic signal than expected under BM. However, the significance testing is not versus a value of 1.0, but rather relative to random associations of data and phylogeny. In other words, one shuffles the data on the tips of the phylogeny and compares the observed K (or Kmult) to that distribution. That distribution of permuted values is not guaranteed to be centered on 1.0, as it depends entirely on the data and the phylogeny. Thus, the significance testing (as described originally for the univariate in Blomberg et al. 2003 and also by me for multivariate Kmult) tests whether the observed K (or Kmult) is greater than one expects given the dataset and the phylogeny.

So it is entirely possible that one has significantly greater phylogenetic signal than expected by chance (where chance is defined as the association of data to tips), but still be less than 1.0: the expected value under BM. Of course, one could devise some way of testing the observed K or Kmult against 1.0; much like one could specify a specific value against which a regression coefficient is compared, but to my knowledge no one has devised and tested such a procedure for phylogenetic signal measures (though I’ve had numerous discussions with some individuals on this topic).

As to your second question, the logic of the interpretation is basically identical.  With PLS we are describing the association of X and Y. With PPLS, we are describing the association of X and Y while accounting for non-independence due to phylogeny. Where you must be careful however is assuming that positive values on a PLS axis means the underlying variable scores are larger, and negative values means the underlying variable scores are smaller. That is not always the case: either with PLS or PPLS (or PCA or some other types of summary axes for that matter).  The reason is that the positive and negative ‘sides’ of summary axes based on eigen-decomposition (or SVD) are completely arbitrary.

The simplest way to think about this is with PCA.  Do a PCA of some data. PC1 defines the direction of greatest variation in the dataset.  There is no natural positive or negative to this: it is just a direction vector. Further, for different computer algorithms for finding PC1, using the same input data you could find the same exact PC1, but the +/- side could be flipped between algorithms. This is not a failing of the math, but rather just a recognition that the sign is arbitrary.  Same thing for PLS axes. So what that means is that one must actually look at the data to determine whether the ‘+’ side of a PCA or PLS vector associates with larger or smaller values of the original variables; one cannot assume it is the case for any dataset.

For the case of PLS and PPLS, the important step you should probably include is this last one: take the time to go back and look at your original variables relative to PLS 1 and PPLS 1. This will tell you how to interpret changes along the axis.

Best,

Dean

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I hope it's been a happy holiday season for all.

I have a question about how to specify the level of replication in gpagen and other functions in geomorph.

The problem I face is the following:

Specifically, I have samples from 11 populations (5 from habitat type A, 6 from habitat type B), with approximately 60-90 individuals from each population and all are identified as male or female.

My first question is, how can I compute separate mean (consensus) configurations and standard errors for each habitat type, such that each one is a mean of the population means? I understand that gpagen computes the mean configuration for each group (in my case, habitat type) by pooling individuals within that group, ignoring the population factor. So in other words, can  gpagen be used to compute a mean of the population means, as well as standard errors? If not, would it be legitimate to repeat the process twice? (i.e. once for each population, then again for each habitat type using population means).

Also, if the above is possible, would it be anymore complicated to do this separately for males and females in each habitat type?

I know that in procD.lm and advanced.procD.lm, I can specify at least two factors, but as far as I can see, the mean configuration is computed by pooling individuals at the specified level.

My concern over this is because I have been advised to use the mean of means for my analyses to avoid issues with pseudo-replication. Also, it seems that pooling individuals from all populations within a habitat type is not advisable because of the obvious effect that sample size has on standard errors, especially if the mean +/- se is computed for 5 observations vs 500 observations.

Looking forward to your responses.

Kind regards,

Daniel

Hi Daniel,

To calculate the mean shape for a group, simply use the geomorph::mshape function as follows (using a geomorph example):

data(plethodon)

Y.gpa <- gpagen(plethodon$land,PrinAxes=FALSE) # perform GPA

# get mean shapes for the two species in plethodon$species factor

plethodon$species

 [1] Jord  Jord  Jord  Jord  Jord  Jord  Jord  Jord  Jord  Jord  Teyah Teyah Teyah Teyah Teyah

[16] Teyah Teyah Teyah Teyah Teyah Jord  Jord  Jord  Jord  Jord  Jord  Jord  Jord  Jord  Jord

[31] Teyah Teyah Teyah Teyah Teyah Teyah Teyah Teyah Teyah Teyah

Levels: Jord Teyah

mean.Jord <- mshape(Y.gpa$coords[,,which(plethodon$species == "Jord")])

mean.Teyah <- mshape(Y.gpa$coords[,,which(plethodon$species == "Teyah")])

# Or using the function geomorph::coords.subset

new.coords <- coords.subset(A = Y.gpa$coords, group = plethodon$species)

# new.coords is a list length 2, with two 3D arrays for the two levels, named by the level name, so:

mean.Jord <- mshape(new.coords$Jord)

mean.Teyah <- mshape(new.coords$Teyah)

# To view:

plotRefToTarget(mean.Jord, mean.Jord, method = "points") # mean shape on own

plotRefToTarget(Y.gpa$consensus, mean.Jord, method = "TPS") # as a shape change from the overall mean

Emma

And yet a third way to do the same thing…

Use coords.subset and mshape

data("plethodon")
Y.gpa <- gpagen(plethodon$land)
lapply(coords.subset(Y.gpa$coords, plethodon$species), mshape)

One could also quickly get means from separate GPAs done individually on groups

groupGPAs <- lapply(coords.subset(plethodon$land, plethodon$species), mshape)
groupGPAs

Of note, if one did the latter, the landmark VCVs could be extracted and SEs could be calculated, but any interpretation form such a thing should be done with caution.  In this case, landmark SEs are not purely attributed to natural variation at landmarks, but also the GPA procedure, itself.

Mike

Rob,

This analysis should be treated as a factorial model, not a nested on.  There are several reasons for why one generally considers sex as a main effect and not a nested term within species, which I won’t enumerate here. However, one very important  reason is related to your biological question: are there species-specific difference among the sexes?

That question is embodied in and characterized by the interaction term of the model, and nested models do not have an interaction term.  This SS is subsumed into the nested term of the model, so one cannot evaluate it individually.

To address your question you need a full factorial model. If you look a bit further down the help file for advanced.procD.lm there should be an example. It will contain post-hoc tests of (in your case) a 4 x 4 set of pairwise comparisons. A significant interaction term in the model implies species-specific sexual dimorphism, and the pairwise comparisons provide ONE test of potential differences.

NOTE: if the interaction term is significant there could be other reasons why that do not show up in ‘classical’ post-hoc tests. Standard post-hoc tests evaluate the distance between population means; that is the magnitude of shape difference. But there could also be a directional difference in morphospace.  Some years ago we developed trajectory analysis precisely for this reason (see Collyer and Adams 2007; Adams and Collyer 2007; Adams and Collyer 2009, etc.).  The function trajectory.analysis in geomorph will facilitate this further analysis.

Best,

Dean

Robin,

This is a curious result.  The first question I must ask is how recently have you updated geomorph?  We had a bug like this that we fixed  a while back.

Assuming that you have recently updated geomorph, it is possible (though unlikely) for a result like this.  First, notice that your Rsq, F, and Z values are all quite small.  The interaction is not a strong effect, even if the SS is significantly greater than 0.  It is possible for many small pairwise distances to accumulatively have a significant effect.  The question is, does it matter?  If the interaction only explains 1.5% of the overall variation in shape, is it it meaningful and should you bother with any multiple comparisons test?

Nonetheless, your pairwise P-values are not even borderline, so it suggests that there is a programming glitch.  If you have not updated geomorph recently, I recommend doing so via our github repository.  If you have, we might have to investigate this further to see if there is a problem.

Cheers!
Mike

Dear Robin and all geomorph users,

Robin’s issue of having a significant but small interaction effect, but also having no significant pairwise differences, got me to wondering how a type I error might manifest in terms of pairwise comparisons.  I decided to simulate data and run the same tests Robin performed.  I did two simulations: 1) where there were significant main effects, but no interaction and 2) where there were significant main effects plus a significant interaction.  When simulating data like these, in the case of the former, I could choose times when an interaction just happened to be significant, even though it should not be.  This is a type I error (just from random sampling).  In each case that this happened, the effect was small but significant, and when I ran advanced.procD.lm for pairwise comparisons, none were significant, just like Robin found.  When I simulated a meaningful interaction, the interaction was significant each time, and some pairwise comparisons were also significant.

There is a lesson to learn here.

Hinging inferences on P-values from results is dangerous.  This might be especially true for highly multivariate data.  In Robin’s case, she found that an interaction that explained 1.5% of the shape variation was “significant”.  That means that in the 1000 permutations she used, never was there SS for the interaction that exceeded her observed case.  But that does not mean the SS was large.  This is why we provide Rsq and effect sizes (Z scores) for all of our statistics.  It allows one to use multiple criteria for deciding if a result is biologically significant, rather than merely statistically significant.

Another, more simple analogy to consider this problem is to think of size, not shape.  Let’s say hypothetically that females are just slightly smaller in Robin’s A group and just slightly larger than males in her T group.  In each case, there is not sexual dimorphism.  But these small, but not significant effects could combine to produce a small but significant sex x ancestry effect, even though no pairwise comparisons are significant.  (This problem might be exacerbated with many shape variables.)

Finally, Robin, it is worth pointing out that you performed a test with ~ ancestry + sex as the null model.  This means you did not find any significant pairwise differences with respect to general factor-level differences.  For example, sexual dimorphism in A and T groups were both no different than sexual dimorphism for both groups combined.  If you had just used an intercept as a null model (~ 1), you would surely find significant pairwise distances.  So your result does not mean there is not significant sexual dimorphism; it just means that the sexual dimorphisms in each group do not differ from overall sexual dimorphism.

I hope that helps wrap up this analytical paradox for you.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Daniel,

We did in fact understand your original question and its intent. Our responses were framed the way they were because what you wished to do and thought was an obvious way to go is not statistically legitimate, nor is it necessary.

Simply put, one should not perform separate GPA – superimpositions on different groups and then combine these data or some summaries of them in downstream analyses. That is the case for the individuals, or the means based on them. The reason is that each GPA will superimpose specimens to their own mean, but these are not aligned to an overall mean.  Thus, each dataset is a projected to a different rotation (projection) in tangent space, making them incompatible for subsequent analyses (see papers by Rohlf in the 1990s where this is discussed).

So instead, if one is interested in population means (or means from any grouping), the correct approach is to perform GPA on all specimens and then obtain group means from these aligned specimens. These will contain all of the shape differences between group means, which is embodied by their Procrustes distances to each other.

Interestingly, it turns out that nothing is gained by performing the second GPA on the group means obtained by first doing GPA on everyone.  If you keep the data in Shape space (not Tangent space), the correlation of distances between the original means, and the GPA-rotated means is precisely 1.0!  If you use the Tangent space coordinates, it won’t be exactly 1.0, but will be extremely close (~0.9998 or so), which reflects the projection-scaling step from Shape Space to Tangent Space.  R-code example is below for you.

So you see, the steps you wished to perform are superfluous, and one can get to where you wished to go using a single GPA of all specimens, followed by the calculation of group means from them.

Hope this makes things more clear.

Dean

library(geomorph)

data(plethodon)

Y.gpa<-gpagen(plethodon$land,Proj=FALSE)    #GPA-alignment

gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(Y.gpa, species = plethodon$species, site = plethodon$site)

means<-advanced.procD.lm(coords ~ site*species, ~ 1, groups = ~site*species,

                  iter=499, data = gdf)$LS.means

orig<-dist(means)

new<-dist(two.d.array(gpagen(arrayspecs(means,p=12,k=2),Proj=FALSE)$coords))

cor(orig,new)

messages.body_plain:
Milena,

What your analysis tells you is that the PopulationSex effect is significant with reference to the PopulationSex:Tree effect.  Normally, the F value is found as MS PopulationSex / MS Residuals (notice that the MS for residuals is 17.53, which is a lot smaller than MS for PopulationSex:Tree).  This would be a huge value and potentially pseudoreplication, as your observational units should be trees.  The nested update changes the F value to be MS PopulationSex / MS PopulationSex:Tree, which in this case is still highly significant.  Meaning = The variation among population x sex groups is large relative to the variation among trees within groups.

The table you want is not something nested.update is currently sophisticated enough to do.  However, if PopulationSex is significant, then it means the combination of Population, Sex, and their interaction are significant.

Finding tree means and using a simpler analysis is also something else you can do if you have balanced data (equal number of trees per group).

Agh. You have the same names for multiple taxa. That will cause errors for all phylogeny-related R packages, as they don’t know which data point corresponds to which tip of the phylogeny.

You will need to make unique names in your dataset and your phylogeny, then have a 1-to-1 correspondence.

HINT: a good check for this is the function ‘treedata’ in geiger. It will match the tree and the data and prune them both to match. In looking at what is pruned out of the tree or the data matrix, you can find errors in your labels more easily.

> Dear Robin and all geomorph users,
>
> Robin’s issue of having a significant but small interaction effect, but also having no significant pairwise differences, got me to wondering how a type I error might manifest in terms of pairwise comparisons.  I decided to simulate data and run the same tests Robin performed.  I did two simulations: 1) where there were significant main effects, but no interaction and 2) where there were significant main effects plus a significant interaction.  When simulating data like these, in the case of the former, I could choose times when an interaction just happened to be significant, even though it should not be.  This is a type I error (just from random sampling).  In each case that this happened, the effect was small but significant, and when I ran advanced.procD.lm for pairwise comparisons, none were significant, just like Robin found.  When I simulated a meaningful interaction, the interaction was significant each time, and some pairwise comparisons were also significant.
>
> There is a lesson to learn here.
>
> Hinging inferences on P-values from results is dangerous.  This might be especially true for highly multivariate data.  In Robin’s case, she found that an interaction that explained 1.5% of the shape variation was “significant”.  That means that in the 1000 permutations she used, never was there SS for the interaction that exceeded her observed case.  But that does not mean the SS was large.  This is why we provide Rsq and effect sizes (Z scores) for all of our statistics.  It allows one to use multiple criteria for deciding if a result is biologically significant, rather than merely statistically significant.
>
> Another, more simple analogy to consider this problem is to think of size, not shape.  Let’s say hypothetically that females are just slightly smaller in Robin’s A group and just slightly larger than males in her T group.  In each case, there is not sexual dimorphism.  But these small, but not significant effects could combine to produce a small but significant sex x ancestry effect, even though no pairwise comparisons are significant.  (This problem might be exacerbated with many shape variables.)
>
> Finally, Robin, it is worth pointing out that you performed a test with ~ ancestry + sex as the null model.  This means you did not find any significant pairwise differences with respect to general factor-level differences.  For example, sexual dimorphism in A and T groups were both no different than sexual dimorphism for both groups combined.  If you had just used an intercept as a null model (~ 1), you would surely find significant pairwise distances.  So your result does not mean there is not significant sexual dimorphism; it just means that the sexual dimorphisms in each group do not differ from overall sexual dimorphism.
>
> I hope that helps wrap up this analytical paradox for you.
>
> Cheers!
> Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

After reading Milena's post about nested ANOVA designs, I went and dug into the help files for nested.update and both procD.lm and advanced.procD.lm functions.

Something stood out for me in the nested.update examples provided in its help file.

One example states the following:

tailANOVA <- proc.D(coord ~ Csize * Treatment/Family, iter=99, RRPP=TRUE, data=gdf)

# This will not work: tailANOVA<- nested.update ( tailANOVA, ~ Treatment/Family)

Does this mean that a nested design cannot include an interaction effect?

If my data originate from a two factor experimental design (e.g. one random factor which is not of interest, (site) nested within a fixed factor (species)) could I specify a model that takes this hierchical design into account, and tests an interaction of species with another fixed factor such as sex?

In other words, would the following model work?

coords ~ (species/site) * sex

If not, how could one specify such a design that would work with procD,lm and nested.update? And can this be done using an ANOVA based analysis at all?

Looking forward to your response.

Regards,

messages.body_plain:
Daniel,

It’s not that other designs cannot be done, in principle, but currently, nested.update cannot do something more complicated than a single factor nested within another.  The programming required to account for all manner of interactions is a Herculean task to accomplish.

One thing to point out, the model you suggested looks simple, but is really: coords ~ species + sex + species:site + species:sex + species:site:sex.

So my question is, what should be the random effect for each F value in ANOVA?  Is it really straightforward?

If someone wants to tangle with that, the beautiful thing is that procD.lm produces the SS for each term, for every random permutation.  So, there is the opportunity to calculate the F values, as desired, provided one can manage doing it “by hand”.  It is perhaps only a few lines of code.  For the few cases where somebody has this need, it is easier to offer suggestions for such programming than it is to anticipate all permutations of interactions with the nested.update function.  (Consider this an optimal efficiency model.)

So, specifically for your example, if you want the F value for species:sex to be MS species:sex / MS species:site:sex, something like this can be done

fit <- procD.lm(coords ~ (species/site) * sex)

fit$random.SS # all random outcomes
fit$df # df for each effect

random.MS.ranef <- fit$random.SS[5,]/fit$df[5]
random.MS.fixed <- fit$random.SS[4,]/fit$df[4]
random.Fs <- random.MS.fixed/random.MS.ranef

random.Fs[1] # observed F
geomorph:::pval(random.Fs) # P-value
geomorph:::effect.size(random.Fs) # Z score

You could then replace the F, Z, and P values in the procD.lm ANOVA output with these values.  You could follow the same procedure for any row in the ANOVA table divided by any other row.

With any single factor nested by another factor, it is easy to search the terms of the linear model and find which row gets divided by which other row.  Once there is an interaction, the programming is sufficiently difficult and is not something I have yet worked up the courage to attempt.  This email response is frankly much easier.

Hope that makes sense,

Mike

Daniel,

If it were me, I would take a look at the model. e.g.,

terms(~(species/site) * sex)

And I would try to determine what the expected mean squares (EMS) is for each term.  I would then make sure my F-values were calculated with respect to the EMS (choose the right denominator).  This is pretty simple for single interactions in mixed models (i.e., one nested factor).  If A is fixed and B is random, then F values are calculated as F for A = MSA/MSAB, F for B = MSB/MSE, and F for AB  = MSAB/MSE.  Once there is a three way interaction, things get interesting.

I found this via a quick search.  It is from Jorge Dubcovsky, a plant scientist at UC-Davis.  I believe these are notes from an experimental design course.

http://www.plantsciences.ucdavis.edu/agr205/Lectures/2011_Lectures/L10_MixModels.pdf

If you follow the logic to the point where he discusses three-way interactions, you will see that “what to do?” becomes less straightforward.  The simplest answer appears to be if you have a single fixed effect, calculate F by dividing by MS for a two-way interaction including the fixed effect with the random effect.  If you have a two-way interaction between fixed effects, divide by the MS for the three-way interaction (like I did in the example).  But there is another example with adding the MS for two-way interactions and subtracting the MS for the three-way interaction.  I’ll cite exactly what Dubcovsky said in this document: "In factorial experiments with three or more factors, at least one of which is a random factor, and certain other, more complex designs, there are frequently no exact test statistics for certain effects in the models.”  In other words, you have strayed into territory where there is no single correct approach.

If I were in your shoes, I would be inclined (mostly by ease in approach and interpretation) to calculate F values as

species: MS species / MS species:site:sex (probably easiest) or MS species / MS species:site
site: MS site/ MSE
sex: MS sex / MS species:site:sex
species:sex: MS species:sex / MS species:site:sex
species:site:sex: MS species:site:sex / MSE

Note that all random effects are divided by MSE, all fixed effects by the MS for the highest interaction.

The important thing is that you have to do this across all random permutations and recalculate effects sizes and p-values.  This is not easy, but it can be done.

Again, I hope this demonstrates the increased complexity with more than a single two-way interaction and why nested.update has only a “primitive” approach (say compared to proc MIXED in SAS or lmer in R, which both are designed for univariate data analysis).

Mike

PS I have visualized a future new function or modification of nested.update where users can use the function and indicate the EMS with something like,

error = c(“species:site:sex”, “Residual”, “species:site:sex”, “species:site:sex”, “Residual”)

as an argument, for example, with the terms I used above.  This would only appeal to advanced users who can envision what the EMS should be, and it is not a trivial programming hurdle.  Maybe when I get a sabbatical…

messages.body_plain:
Milena,

Yes, that is correct.

The random.SS in procD.lm (or random.Fs in procD.pgls) is a matrix with dimensions of (Number of effects x Number of random iterations + 1).  The first column of values are the observed SS; the rest of the columns are the SS values for each random permutation.  The observed values are considered the first iteration, as any permutation procedure has to consider the observed case to be one possible random outcome.  We just slot that in position 1.

Mike

> > Daniel,
> >
> > It’s not that other designs cannot be done, in principle, but currently, nested.update cannot do something more complicated than a single factor nested within another.  The programming required to account for all manner of interactions is a Herculean task to accomplish.
> >
> > One thing to point out, the model you suggested looks simple, but is really: coords ~ species + sex + species:site + species:sex + species:site:sex.
> >
> > So my question is, what should be the random effect for each F value in ANOVA?  Is it really straightforward?
> >
> > If someone wants to tangle with that, the beautiful thing is that procD.lm produces the SS for each term, for every random permutation.  So, there is the opportunity to calculate the F values, as desired, provided one can manage doing it “by hand”.  It is perhaps only a few lines of code.  For the few cases where somebody has this need, it is easier to offer suggestions for such programming than it is to anticipate all permutations of interactions with the nested.update function.  (Consider this an optimal efficiency model.)
> >
> > So, specifically for your example, if you want the F value for species:sex to be MS species:sex / MS species:site:sex, something like this can be done
> >
> > fit <- procD.lm(coords ~ (species/site) * sex)
> >
> > fit$random.SS # all random outcomes
> > fit$df # df for each effect
> >
> > random.MS.ranef <- fit$random.SS[5,]/fit$df[5]
> > random.MS.fixed <- fit$random.SS[4,]/fit$df[4]
> > random.Fs <- random.MS.fixed/random.MS.ranef
> >
> > random.Fs[1] # observed F
> > geomorph:::pval(random.Fs) # P-value
> > geomorph:::effect.size(random.Fs) # Z score
> >
> > You could then replace the F, Z, and P values in the procD.lm ANOVA output with these values.  You could follow the same procedure for any row in the ANOVA table divided by any other row.
> >
> > With any single factor nested by another factor, it is easy to search the terms of the linear model and find which row gets divided by which other row.  Once there is an interaction, the programming is sufficiently difficult and is not something I have yet worked up the courage to attempt.  This email response is frankly much easier.
